summary: JMAP is a JSON-based protocol for mail and related data, and it can send Web Push notifications to clients. This RFC defines how a JMAP server can advertise that it supports authenticating those pushes using VAPID, so clients can tell the notifications really come from their server.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9749 lets a JMAP server tell clients which public key it uses to authenticate Web Push notifications. Clients give that key to the push service and need to recreate subscriptions when the server changes keys.

subtitle: How JMAP clients discover and use a server's VAPID key for Web Push.

tldr.problem: Some push services require application servers to authenticate push messages, so a JMAP client needs the server's VAPID public key when it creates a push subscription.
tldr.mechanism: A JMAP session advertises the capability urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid and its applicationServerKey. The server authenticates each push using a token signed by the matching private key.
tldr.outcome: Clients can create authenticated push subscriptions and detect key changes. RFC 9749 is a Proposed Standard and has not been replaced.

today: RFC 9749 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why JMAP Advertises a VAPID Key
sections.content: JMAP clients can subscribe to events using a protocol compatible with Web Push. Some push services require the application server to authenticate every push message with VAPID. The client therefore needs the server's public key to pass to the push service when it retrieves a new endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: A push service may require proof of who sent a notification. The JMAP client needs the server's public key when it creates a push subscription.

sections.title: Discovering and Using the Key
sections.content:
A supporting server must add urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid to the capabilities object in its JMAP session. That capability contains applicationServerKey, an uncompressed ECDSA public key encoded with base64url. Current systems use the P-256 curve, and the format is compatible with the browser Push API.

For every push to a PushSubscription URL, including StateChange and PushVerification notifications, the server must authenticate the POST using VAPID. It uses a JSON Web Token signed by the private key matching the key advertised when that subscription was created.
sections.plainLanguage: The session tells the client the server's public key. The server signs each push with the matching private key, so the push service can check it.

sections.title: Replacing a VAPID Key
sections.content:
When a server replaces its key, it must update sessionState. The client must monitor the session for the change and recreate its push subscription. The server may keep using the old key for a transition period, but it must destroy subscriptions using that key when the period ends. It may send a final StateChange push to prompt the client to check for changes.

A race can occur if the server changes keys after the client refreshed its session but before it creates a subscription. The push service then rejects a PushVerification with status 403. The client must check that the returned sessionState contains the expected key; it may retry or destroy the failed subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server changes keys, the client needs to refresh its subscription. If the change happens during setup, the push service can reject a verification message, so the client checks the returned session state.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
A subscription tied to an old key can cause a PushVerification signed with the new key to be rejected with status 403. The server must not retry that rejected request, so the client is responsible for detecting and resolving synchronization problems.

The advertised capability says only that the server supports VAPID. The RFC says it does not reveal sensitive information or add security or privacy risks beyond those already associated with JMAP and Web Push. IANA registered the capability with intended use common.
sections.plainLanguage: A key change can make a verification push fail, and the server does not retry it. The client must notice and resolve the mismatch.
